letters.name: a
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 'u' in English 'but' or a short 'a' as in 'father'. Keep it open and relaxed — never like the 'a' in 'cat'.

letters.name: dlouhé a (long a)
letters.memoryTrick: Just like 'a' but held about twice as long — like the 'a' in 'father' drawn out. The acute accent means 'stretch this vowel.'

letters.name: bé
letters.memoryTrick: Exactly like English 'b'. At the end of a word it devoices to a 'p' sound — 'dub' (oak) sounds like 'dup'.

letters.name: cé
letters.memoryTrick: Always 'ts' as in 'cats' — never like 'k' or 's' alone. Imagine the double sound at the end of 'pizza' without the 'i'.

letters.name: čé
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'ch' in English 'chair' or 'church'. The little hook (caron / háček) turns a plain 'ts' into a 'ch'.

letters.name: dé
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'd' but dental — put your tongue against the back of your upper teeth. At the end of a word it devoices to 't'.

letters.name: ďé
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'd' in British 'duty' or 'duke' — the tongue presses up against the hard palate. Try saying 'dy' with your tongue arched high, almost like a soft 'gy' sound.

letters.name: é
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'e' in English 'bet' or 'bed'. A clean, open short vowel — never silent at the end of a word like in English.

letters.name: dlouhé e (long e)
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'e' in 'bet' but held longer — similar to 'air' in English without the 'r' at the end. The acute accent stretches the vowel.

letters.name: ě (e s háčkem)
letters.memoryTrick: Never at the start of a word. After b, p, v, f it adds a 'y' glide (like 'bye'). After d, t, n it palatalizes them — 'dě' sounds like 'dyeh'. After m it sounds like 'mnye'.

letters.name: ef
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'f'. Appears mostly in loanwords — native Czech words rarely use 'f'.

letters.name: gé
letters.memoryTrick: Always hard like 'g' in 'go' — never soft like 'g' in 'gem'. Mostly in loanwords; native Czech words with 'g' are rare.

letters.name: há
letters.memoryTrick: A voiced, breathy 'h' — like the 'h' in English 'behind' or 'ahead'. Unlike English 'h' in 'hat', your vocal cords should vibrate softly.

letters.name: chá
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'ch' in Scottish 'loch' or German 'Bach' — a rough throat sound. It is a single letter in Czech, sorted after 'h'. Not like English 'ch' in 'chair'.

letters.name: i (měkké i)
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'i' in English 'bit' — short and crisp. Called 'měkké i' (soft i) because it palatalizes the preceding d, t, n (turns them into ď, ť, ň sounds).

letters.name: dlouhé i (long i)
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'ee' in English 'see' or 'feel' — a long, pure vowel. Hold it longer than short 'i'. Also called 'dlouhé měkké í'.

letters.name: jé
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'y' in English 'yes' or 'yogurt'. Always a consonant, never like the English 'j' in 'jam'.

letters.name: ká
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'k' in English 'skip' — unaspirated (no puff of air). Unlike English 'k' in 'key', keep it crisp without the breath.

letters.name: el
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'l' but never the 'dark l' of English 'milk'. Keep your tongue tip behind your upper teeth — it stays light and clear in all positions.

letters.name: em
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'm'. Unlike some languages, Czech 'm' before 'ě' adds a 'ň' sound: 'mě' sounds like 'mnye' in 'město' (city).

letters.name: en
letters.memoryTrick: Like English 'n' but dental — tongue tip touches the back of your upper teeth. Before 'i' and 'í' it palatalizes to 'ň'.

letters.name: eň
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'ny' in 'canyon' or Spanish 'ñ' in 'señor'. Press the middle of your tongue up against your hard palate. Very rare at the start of words.

letters.name: ó
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'o' in British English 'hot' — a clean, open short vowel. Never diphthongized like the American 'o' in 'go'.

letters.name: dlouhé o (long o)
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'o' held longer — a rare letter in Czech, found mainly in loanwords. Sounds a bit like the 'o' in English 'go' but without the 'w' glide at the end.

letters.name: pé
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'p' in English 'spin' — unaspirated, no puff of air. Crisp and clean, not breathy like the 'p' in 'pin'.

letters.name: kvé
letters.memoryTrick: Extremely rare in Czech — appears only in foreign words. Pronounced like 'kv'. Think of 'queen' but shortened to just the 'kw' part.

words.meaning: quasi — note: spelled with 'kv' in native Czech

letters.name: er
letters.memoryTrick: A rolled/flapped 'r' — like in Spanish or Italian. Tap the tip of your tongue against the ridge behind your upper teeth. Czech 'r' can even act as a vowel, as in 'krk' (neck).

letters.name: eř
letters.memoryTrick: The famous Czech ř — unique to the language! Try rolling an 'r' while simultaneously saying 'zh' (like the 's' in 'measure'). It's a raised alveolar fricative trill: the tongue vibrates like an 'r' but with friction like a 'zh'.

letters.name: es
letters.memoryTrick: Like 's' in English 'sun' — always voiceless. Unlike in English, Czech 's' never sounds like 'z' between vowels.

letters.name: eš
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'sh' in English 'shoe' or 'ship'. The háček (little hook) above 's' signals the shift from a plain 's' to 'sh'.

letters.name: té
letters.memoryTrick: Like 't' in English 'stop' — unaspirated (no puff of air). Dental: place your tongue against the back of your upper teeth, not the ridge behind them.

letters.name: ťé
letters.memoryTrick: Like 't' in British English 'tune' — a palatal 't'. Your tongue touches both your upper teeth and the hard palate at the same time. Try saying 'ty' with a very high tongue arch.

letters.name: ú
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'oo' in English 'book' or 'foot' — short and rounded. Keep your lips tightly rounded; don't relax them like in English 'put'.

letters.name: dlouhé u (long u)
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'oo' in English 'moon' — long and round. Found almost only at the beginning of words and in prefixes. The same sound as ů, but ů appears in the middle/end of words.

letters.name: ů (u s kroužkem)
letters.memoryTrick: Same sound as ú (long 'oo' as in 'moon'), but NEVER at the start of a word. The little circle (kroužek) is a historical trace — it evolved from an old 'uo' diphthong. Found only in the middle or end of words.

letters.name: vé
letters.memoryTrick: Same as English 'v'. At the end of a word it devoices to 'f' — so 'lev' (lion) is pronounced 'lef'.

letters.name: dvojité vé
letters.memoryTrick: Only in loanwords — pronounced just like Czech 'v'. Called 'dvojité vé' (double v). Think of it as a fancy 'v' that only appears in foreign words.

letters.name: iks
letters.memoryTrick: Only in loanwords. Pronounced like 'ks' — identical to English 'x' in 'box'. Very rare in Czech; most words with this sound are spelled with 'ks' instead.

letters.name: ypsilon (tvrdé y)
letters.memoryTrick: Sounds exactly the same as short 'i' (like 'i' in 'bit'), but called 'tvrdé y' (hard y) because it does NOT palatalize the preceding d, t, n — they stay hard. Knowing when to write 'i' vs 'y' is famously tricky in Czech!

letters.name: dlouhé ypsilon (long y)
letters.memoryTrick: Same sound as long í (like 'ee' in 'see'), but called 'dlouhé tvrdé ý' — the hard counterpart. Preceding d, t, n stay hard before ý. The long mark plus ypsilon signals hardness plus length.

letters.name: zet
letters.memoryTrick: Like 'z' in English 'zoo'. At the end of a word it devoices to 's' — so 'vůz' (wagon) sounds like 'voos'.

letters.name: žet
letters.memoryTrick: Like the 's' in English 'measure' or 'pleasure', or the French 'j' in 'je'. A voiced 'sh' — your vocal cords vibrate. The háček turns 'z' into 'zh'.
